analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a warrant to read stored emails and to track a phone's location.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill requiring warrants for stored emails and phone location data was referred to the Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill updated a 1980s-era privacy law to match how people actually communicate today. It would require police to get a judge's warrant before reading emails or other stored communications held by a provider like Gmail or Verizon, and before obtaining location data showing where a phone has been. It would also generally require the government to tell people within 10 business days after their communications or location data were taken, allow courts to suppress evidence gathered in violation of the rules, and order public reports on law enforcement's use of cell-site simulators ("stingrays").
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses email, cloud storage, or a cell phone. The bill would close a loophole in the existing law (ECPA) under which email stored more than 180 days can be obtained without a warrant, and would extend warrant protection to location data, which the current law does not clearly cover. It would also let criminal defendants suppress evidence obtained in violation of the new rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a warrant for any stored contents of communications held by a provider, eliminating the rule that email held longer than 180 days needed only a subpoena [S3].
Requires a warrant for stored geolocation information and bars government location tracking of an electronic device except under a warrant, court order, emergencies, or user consent [S3].

Requires the government to notify a subscriber within 10 business days of taking their communications or location data, with court-approved delays of up to 90 days (renewable) for investigations [S3].
Adds a suppression remedy: evidence obtained in violation of the rules, and evidence derived from it, cannot be used in court, and unlawfully collected data must be destroyed [S3].
Tightens the standard for pen register and trap-and-trace orders, requiring specific and articulable facts showing reasonable grounds rather than a mere applicant certification [S3].

Orders FCC and GAO reports on law enforcement's domestic use of cell-site simulators, including who uses them, whether they are used at protests or for immigration enforcement, and whether they disproportionately affect particular communities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies, which would face more paperwork and time in getting warrants instead of subpoenas or court orders for stored data. Providers of email, cloud, and phone services would bear some compliance costs, though the bill compensates them for technical assistance and shields them from lawsuits for helping with authorized acquisitions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and service providers

drawbacks.text: Warrant requirements can slow investigations; the bill mitigates this with emergency and 48-hour provisions, but exigent cases would still involve more process than under current law [S3].
Notification of surveillance can be delayed up to 90 days at a time, repeatedly, and nondisclosure orders can also be extended, so the notice right is not absolute [S3].
The bill leaves other authorities untouched, expressly preserving acquisitions under the Wiretap Act and FISA, so intelligence surveillance and national-security access are largely unaffected [S3].
Service providers get immunity from lawsuits for assisting in authorized acquisitions, which some privacy advocates would view as a meaningful trade-off for the added protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are substantial and general: warrant protection for stored email and phone location is a real limitation on government access to data nearly every American generates daily. The costs fall mainly on law enforcement efficiency and are softened by emergency exceptions and a 48-hour rule. The main structural weakness is the carve-out for other statutes, which leaves much surveillance capacity untouched. On balance the bill traded modest investigative friction for a major expansion of personal privacy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2017 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the ECPA Modernization Act of 2017 on July 27, 2017, joined by Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT) as an original cosponsor [S3, S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or floor consideration before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to obtain stored email and location data through lighter legal process than a warrant, and service providers continue responding to subpoenas and orders under the older, weaker rules. Phone and email users keep fewer protections than the bill would have given them.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring warrants for stored communications and geolocation data

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction; he was a principal author of the original electronic privacy law the bill amends

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or committee vote on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from the start: a Republican sponsor and lead Democratic original cosponsor, with its two additional cosponsors split one Democrat and one Republican; the record shows no organized opposition vote, only committee inaction [S4].

industries.industry: Law enforcement and surveillance (police agencies; cell-site simulator vendors)
industries.note: Agencies would need warrants and to give notice for stored communications and location tracking, and the bill would have produced public reports on stingray use, including at protests and in immigration enforcement. Their interest in continuing current access runs against the privacy of ordinary people.

The bill imposes compliance duties and a notice interface with government, but also gives providers a single clear warrant standard, reimburses technical assistance, and shields them from lawsuits for helping with authorized acquisitions. Their privacy commitments to customers point the same direction as the bill.
